about.title: About EarthChestra
about.intro: EarthChestra turns Earth data, mostly from NASA, into orchestral music. Choose a place on Earth, listen to how it has changed over time, and watch the data on the globe as the music plays.
about.howZone: Choose a zone on the globe or in the list: a continent, a country, an ocean or a sea.
about.howTracks: Select Sounds to open the "What do you want to hear?" panel and choose the datasets to hear. Each dataset is played by its own instrument.
about.howPlay: Press Play. Each dataset is averaged over your zone, month by month, and every month becomes one bar of music. Use the date button to go to a given month, and Graph to see your zone's values as a chart.
about.howMonths: In Time travel, the Months menu plays one month year after year (for example every July), to hear how the same season changes; choose "Every month" to go back.
about.howPitch: Higher values play higher notes, measured against your zone's own range, so a value always gives the same note.
about.howLoudness: Rain, snow, lightning, fires, night lights and sea ice only play when there is enough of them. The more there is, the louder their instrument plays: heavy rain makes the violins repeat their notes faster, more lightning means more timpani strokes per beat, and the trombones swell with the fires. Night lights change once a year: the synth pad starts clearly each January, then fades slowly over the year.
about.howGaps: When a dataset has no data for a date (for example CO₂ before September 2002), its instrument stays silent.
about.howPeriod: The timeline starts in 1920. Only one dataset, the temperature anomaly, goes further back (to 1880), so we start there to keep the app easier to use. We chose about 100 years so that the dates cover the lifetime of almost everyone alive today.
about.howGlobe: While the music plays, the globe shows the data of your zone as spots: one colour per dataset, and the stronger the value, the bigger the spot. Where there is nothing, there is no spot, so spots appear, grow and fade as the months go by. Temperature is a filled spot when warmer than normal and a ring when colder. Select Change zone or press Escape to pick another zone.
about.orchestraText: In the Orchestra style, each dataset has its own instrument (other styles use their own instruments):
about.dataText: The datasets' map files share one grid of 0.25°, so a place has the same position in every dataset.

sources.gistemp: monthly surface temperature anomaly (°C), January 1880 to December 2025 (shown from January 1920 in the app).
sources.imerg: rain and snow (snow as melted water), monthly means of the daily precipitation rate, June 2000 to November 2026.
sources.lis: share of each map pixel with lightning, monthly, between 55°S and 55°N, March 2017 to July 2023.
sources.modis: days of the month with at least one fire detected (Terra and Aqua), July 2002 to November 2026.
sources.nightLights: night-time lights, brightness from 0 to 1, one map per year from 2012 to 2023; each year's map is used for its 12 months.
sources.nsidc: share of the sea covered by ice (%), monthly, January 1979 to October 2026.
sources.co2: monthly CO₂ concentration (ppm), extracted by the team, September 2002 to March 2022.
sources.modisNdvi: vegetation greenness (NDVI, from −0.2 to 1), monthly, March 2000 to October 2026; the ocean has no value.
sources.mopitt: carbon monoxide in the whole air column (×10¹⁸ molecules/cm²), monthly, April 2000 to October 2024; 20 months are missing at NASA.
sources.oceanColor: ocean chlorophyll-a concentration (mg/m³), monthly geometric mean, July 2002 to October 2026; land and cloud-covered sea have no value.
sources.naturalEarth: outlines of continents, countries, oceans and seas (public domain).

about.techFrontend: Web app: React, TypeScript and Vite. The 3D globe uses react-globe.gl (three.js), and the sound plays through the Web Audio API.
about.techBackend: Music: a Python service (FastAPI) averages each dataset over your zone, on maps reduced to 1° (2° for temperature), writes an orchestral score (MIDI) and renders it to MP3, in pieces that play back to back.
about.techData: Globe: the browser reads the datasets' map files (NumPy) straight from the server and downloads only the part that covers your zone.
about.techDeploy: Deployment: Docker Compose runs the web app (nginx), the music service and a container that installs the datasets. On a small server, the datasets can instead be read from a folder on the server.
about.a11yText: EarthChestra aims to meet WCAG 2.1 AA. All controls can be used with the keyboard. In the player, Space plays or pauses, the arrow keys move through time, Home and End jump to the start or the end, and M mutes. During playback, Escape returns to zone selection. The List View is a screen-reader-friendly alternative to the globe, the values shown on the globe are also available as a table, and status changes are announced.
about.teamText: Built at HEIG-VD (Yverdon-les-Bains, Switzerland) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
about.teamMembers: Magali Egger, Téo Ferrari, Clarisse Estelle Fleurimont, Yasaman Izadmehr, Simon Walther and Léo Zmoos.
about.howStyle: Music style lets you choose how the data is played: orchestra, ragtime, swing, rock'n'roll, funk, synth-pop, house, trap, or recorded sounds of rain, fire and thunder. The global CO₂ sets the tempo, so the number of months in each 30-second stretch changes with the style and the data.
about.howVinyl: Vinyl mode plays the data as a record: the needle can travel through space (one date, the needle crosses places), through time (one place, the months go by) or both (the needle crosses places and the date moves on each groove).
